1	# Writing style — comments, help text, and CLI output
2	
3	This file is the house style for everything a reader sees: Go doc comments,
4	`--help` output, and the strings a command prints or returns as errors. It
5	applies to every Go file in this repository. Keep it short enough that it can
6	be re-read before every PR.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Code comments
11	
12	**Explain why, not what changed.** A comment answers the question the code
13	cannot: the invariant, the trade-off, the reason a non-obvious choice is the
14	safe one. It never narrates history.
15	
16	- Never reference a PR, issue, fix, or the past tense of the code itself.
17	  "Used to", "now", "previously", "after the refactor", "fixes #123" are all
18	  forbidden. Git history already knows; the reader of the code does not care.
19	- A doc comment on every exported symbol. One or two sentences is usually
20	  enough. `golint` enforces this; don't make a reviewer do it.
21	- Target ≤ 10 lines per doc block. If you need more, the extra content
22	  belongs in `docs/` or a README, not above the function.
23	- "Deliberately not X" comments are encouraged when they stop a plausible
24	  wrong refactor. `internal/gitops/remote.go` is the exemplar: it says the
25	  function is *not* used to derive the cache directory, and why.
26	- No TODO, FIXME, HACK, or XXX in committed code. File an issue instead.
27	
28	---
29	
30	## Help text (cobra)
31	
32	`--help` is reference material, not a blog post. A reader in a terminal wants
33	to know what the command does, what it costs, and which flags change the
34	behavior. Philosophy and motivation belong in `docs/`.
35	
36	- **`Short:`** one line, imperative verb, no trailing period.
37	  Good: `Pin a component's image digest into an environment`
38	  Bad:  `This command pins the image digest.`
39	- **`Long:`** target ≤ 150 words, hard ceiling ~200. Cover: what it does,
40	  what it reads, what it writes, what can go wrong that the user can prevent.
41	  Cut: why the command exists, why GitOps is good, architecture essays.
42	- **`Use:`** positional args in `<>`, optional in `[]`, variadic as `name...`.
43	  Good: `pin <component> [version]`
44	  Bad:  `pin COMPONENT [VERSION]`, `pin <component> [<version>]`
45	
46	If a `Long:` draft exceeds 200 words, the excess is almost always the second
47	paragraph onwards. Move it to a file under `docs/` and keep the help text
48	to usage.
49	
50	---
51	
52	## Flag descriptions
53	
54	Use the shared constants in `cmd/intropy/flagtext.go`. Never hand-write a new
55	description for a flag another command already has:
56	
57	- `--output`, `--env`, `--gitops-repo`, `--argocd-server`, `--domain`,
58	  `--system`, `--template-version` all have constants.
59	- If you add a flag that several commands will share, add a constant first.
60	- Flag descriptions are fragments, not sentences: no trailing period, no
61	  "This flag…". Start with the noun. Good: `target environment (required)`.
62	
63	---
64	
65	## Runtime output
66	
67	A CLI's output is read twice: once by a human scanning, once by a script
68	parsing. The two never share a stream.
69	
70	- **stdout is for results.** Tables, JSON, the thing the command was run to
71	  produce.
72	- **stderr is for everything else.** Progress, warnings, completion messages,
73	  errors. A pipeline reading stdout must never see a status line.
74	
75	### Voice
76	
77	- Progress and completion: **lowercase, present tense, no trailing period**.
78	  Good: `syncing api on argocd.example.com at a1b2c3d`
79	  Good: `published ghcr.io/example/releases/api:1.2.0`
80	  Bad:  `Published ghcr.io/…`  `Sync complete.`
81	- Empty states follow the same rule: `no releases found`, not
82	  `No releases found.`
83	- A follow-up hint naming a command goes on its own line, in backticks:
84	  `use 'intropy release create <component>' to publish one`
85	
86	### Errors
87	
88	- Front-load what failed. The remediation, if there is one, goes on a second
89	  line. Do not editorialize — the user is already reading an error.
90	  Good: `pending change is a1b2c3d, not the f4e5d6c you reviewed`
91	        `run 'intropy deploy diff api --env staging' before syncing`
92	  Bad:  `…has advanced since you reviewed it — you really should read the new diff…`
93	- Wrap errors with context as they travel up: `fmt.Errorf("pull %s: %w", …)`.
94	  The outermost prefix names the command or operation, not the internals.
95	
96	### Vocabulary
97	
98	- **image digest**, not "bits", "artifacts", or "the images".
99	- **environment** in prose, `--env` only when naming the flag.
100	- `->` for a transition (`1.0 -> 1.1`), ` @ ` for a pin (`api @ 1.2.0`).
101	  Never mix the two in one message.
102	- A commit SHA is shown short (7 chars) unless the full value is the point.
103	
104	### Command verbs
105	
106	One verb per meaning, used on every noun (`int`, `template`, `deploy`, ...).
107	The full set, grouped by what the verb does to the world:
108	
109	**Read-only** — exit 0 even when the answer is "they disagree", never write
110	to git, never trigger a sync:
111	
112	- **`list`** enumerates a collection: integrations on disk, templates in the
113	  library, published releases. It never prints one item's
114	  details.
115	- **`show`** prints the details of exactly one thing: a template's manifest,
116	  an integration's scaffold record. It never enumerates.
117	- **`status`** reports one component across every environment, one row
118	  each, and whether the rows agree. It never prints one environment's
119	  details — that is `show`.
120	- **`diff`** prints the rendered change a `sync` would apply, as the
121	  resources themselves. Both sides are committed revisions; it never diffs
122	  an uncommitted worktree.
123	- **`inspect`** prints the deployment model derived from one system topology:
124	  components, workloads, ports, and available local fixtures. It never
125	  renders manifests or writes project or Git state.
126	- **`render`** emits a complete Kubernetes YAML stream for one environment.
127	  It may ask for missing local fixture choices, buffers and validates the whole
128	  stream before writing stdout, writes all interaction and diagnostics to
129	  stderr, and never changes project, Git, or cluster state.
130	
131	**Create or change project state** — may write files under the project.
132	Manifest creation may push a review branch, never the default branch:
133	
134	- **`create`** makes something new from a template or from scaffolded
135	  parts: an integration, a system host, a release manifest to publish, or
136	  missing Kubernetes manifests on a GitOps review branch. Manifest creation
137	  accepts existing identical files but never replaces or deletes a file.
138	- **`add`** attaches something that already exists elsewhere to this
139	  project: a library registration. Unlike
140	  `create`, the content is pulled, not generated.
141	- **`update`** reconciles something installed against the ref its source
142	  now pins: a cached index against the registry. It never changes which
143	  ref is pinned — that is the publisher's job.
144	**Move or publish** — change what runs somewhere or what others can pull:
145	
146	- **`publish`** pushes an immutable artifact to an OCI registry: a release
147	  manifest. What is published cannot be edited in
148	  place; a new version is a new publish.
149	- **`pin`** writes one component's image digest into one environment's
150	  overlay.
151	- **`promote`** copies the digests one environment runs into the next
152	  environment in the promotion graph.
153	- **`sync`** applies an environment's pending change through ArgoCD. It
154	  never decides what the change is — that is `pin` and `promote`.
155	
156	Do not import kubectl's `get`/`describe` split — `int describe` was retired
157	because it described templates, not integrations. New verbs need a reason
158	that the set above cannot express, and the reason goes in this file with
159	the verb, not in a commit message.
160	
161	---
162	
163	## What this file is not
164	
165	It does not replace `CONTRIBUTING.md` (workflow, tests, commit convention) or
166	`README.md` (what the CLI is). When those disagree with this file, this file
167	wins on writing style and loses on everything else.
168

1	---
2	date: 2026-01-15
3	topic: config-contexts
4	---
5	
6	# Customer Contexts in the User-Level Config
7	
8	## Problem Frame
9	
10	Developers working across multiple Intropy customers re-specify the same
11	settings — organization, GitOps repository, template library — every time they
12	switch customer, or maintain one global default that is wrong for half their
13	repositories. The settings that identify "which customer am I working for"
14	change together, but today each one is configured independently in
15	`~/.config/intropy/config.yaml`. The file needs named, switchable bundles of
16	these settings, the way kubeconfig binds cluster/user/namespace into a
17	context.
18	
19	## Requirements
20	
21	**Config file format**
22	- R1. `config.yaml` gains a `contexts:` map and a `currentContext:` key. Each
23	  context is a named bundle of the existing settings (`organization`,
24	  `gitopsRepo`, `templateRepo`, `argocdServer`, and any future keys of the
25	  same kind). `organization` is a new top-level/context-level setting — a
26	  plain string whose consumers (scaffolding, image naming) are decided per
27	  consumer, not by this mechanism.
28	- R2. A file with no `contexts:` parses and behaves exactly as today. The
29	  existing flat keys remain valid and become defaults that the active
30	  context's keys override. Nobody who never switches customers needs to learn
31	  the word "context".
32	- R3. Effective precedence: flag > environment > active context > top-level
33	  keys. This extends the existing flag > env > file chain by one rung rather
34	  than replacing it.
35	- R4. Strict parsing extends to the new keys: unknown keys anywhere in the
36	  file are a load error (existing behavior), and a `currentContext` naming a
37	  context absent from `contexts:` is a load error naming the file and the
38	  valid context names.
39	
40	**Switching**
41	- R5. `intropy context use <name>` persists the switch by updating
42	  `currentContext` in the user's config file. The write is surgical: only the
43	  `currentContext` key is created or changed; all other content — comments,
44	  key order, unrelated settings — is preserved byte-for-byte.
45	- R6. `intropy context use <name>` with an unknown name fails, listing the
46	  valid context names.
47	- R7. `intropy context list` prints the configured contexts, marking the
48	  active one. With none configured it prints the empty state
49	  (`no contexts configured`) plus a follow-up hint.
50	- R8. `intropy context show` prints the resolved settings of the active
51	  context — what the CLI is actually pointed at — so a user can verify before
52	  a deploy or scaffold.
53	
54	## Acceptance Examples
55	
56	- AE1. **Covers R2, R3.** Given a config file with only `gitopsRepo:` set and
57	  no `contexts:`, when any existing command runs, then behavior is identical
58	  to today.
59	- AE2. **Covers R1, R3.** Given `templateRepo: acme/intropy-templates` at the
60	  top level and a context `acme` that sets only `gitopsRepo:`, when `acme` is
61	  active, then the effective config uses the context's `gitopsRepo` and the
62	  top-level `templateRepo`.
63	- AE3. **Covers R5, R6.** Given contexts `acme` and `integrio`, when the user
64	  runs `intropy context use acme`, then the file's `currentContext` becomes
65	  `acme` and every subsequent command resolves against `acme` until switched.
66	  `intropy context use acmee` fails and lists `acme` and `integrio`.
67	- AE4. **Covers R5.** Given a config file containing user comments, when
68	  `context use` runs, then the comments are still present afterwards.
69	
70	## Success Criteria
71	
72	- A developer with two customers switches between them with one command, and
73	  scaffolding a component afterwards needs no organization-related input.
74	- A user who never uses contexts experiences zero change in behavior or
75	  documentation burden beyond a skippable new section.
76	- Planning can proceed without inventing user-facing behavior: file shape,
77	  precedence, command surface, and error cases are all specified above.
78	
79	## Scope Boundaries
80	
81	- No repo-level or project-level config file. All settings stay in the
82	  per-user file; layering repo files over it was considered and rejected for
83	  now.
84	- No `--context` flag or `INTROPY_CONTEXT` env var in v1. Persisted switching
85	  only; per-invocation overrides can be added later without breaking
86	  anything.
87	- No creation or editing of contexts by the CLI beyond `currentContext`.
88	  Contexts are authored by hand in the file; the CLI only switches, lists,
89	  and shows.
90	- What `organization` feeds (template parameter defaults, image naming,
91	  GitOps layout) is decided per consumer in separate work; this mechanism
92	  only stores and resolves it.
93	
94	## Key Decisions
95	
96	- Persisted switching (kubectl `use-context` model) over per-session env
97	  vars: the user chose familiarity and one-command switching; the known
98	  "wrong cluster" risk of persisted state is accepted and mitigated by
99	  `context show` (R8) making the active context easy to verify.
100	- Top-level keys stay valid as defaults rather than being deprecated: keeps
101	  single-customer setups at zero ceremony.
102	- The file remains hand-authored and hand-owned: `context use` is the sole
103	  CLI write path, and it changes one key only.
104	
105	## Dependencies / Assumptions
106	
107	- `internal/config` already implements strict YAML loading, flag > env > file
108	  resolution, and "missing file is fine, malformed file is loud" semantics;
109	  this work extends that package rather than adding a new one.
110	- `config.yaml` currently has no `organization` key; it is introduced here.
111	
112	## Next Steps
113	
114	-> /ce-plan for structured implementation planning
115

# intropy CLI

`intropy` is the command-line interface for working with Intropy integrations.
It scaffolds integrations from the official Intropy template library hosted at
[`integrio-intropy/intropy-templates`](https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-templates), then
tracks, deploys, and releases them.

## Install

### Homebrew (macOS)

Distributed as a Homebrew cask (macOS only):

```sh
brew tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew trust --tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew install intropy
```

The `brew trust` step is required when `HOMEBREW_REQUIRE_TAP_TRUST` is set —
the default on current Homebrew (6.x+). On older versions without that
requirement you can skip it.

On Linux, use the quick install script below or download a binary from the
[releases page](https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases).

### Quick install (macOS / Linux)

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

With options:

```sh
# Install to a custom prefix
curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh -s -- --prefix ~/.local

# Install a specific version
curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh -s -- --version v1.0.0
```

The script detects your OS and architecture, downloads the matching release
archive, verifies the SHA256 checksum, optionally verifies the cosign signature,
and installs the binary and shell completions.

### Docker

Multi-arch images (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) are published to GHCR on every
release, built on `distroless/static` and running as a non-root user.

```sh
docker pull ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli:latest

# Scaffolding writes into the working directory: mount your project at /work
# and match your uid so files aren't owned by the container user
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli int create hello-world --name Orders
```

The image contains no shell — the binary is the entrypoint. Images are signed
with cosign; verify with:

```sh
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity-regexp="https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli:latest
```

### From source

Requires Go 1.26+.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli.git
cd intropy-cli
make build
```

Or manually:

```sh
go build -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
```

Add `bin/` to your `PATH`, or move the binary somewhere on your `PATH`.

### Verifying signatures

Release binaries are signed with [cosign](https://sigstore.dev/) using
keyless signing via GitHub Actions OIDC. Each release includes `.sig` and
`.pem` files for every archive.

```sh
# Download the archive, its .sig, and its .pem from the GitHub release
cosign verify-blob \
  --certificate intropy_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz.pem \
  --signature intropy_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz.sig \
  --certificate-identity-regexp="https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  intropy_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz
```

### Windows

Windows is not a supported native target. Install and run `intropy` inside
[WSL 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) using the Linux
instructions above. The CLI relies on Unix path conventions and signal handling
that are not tested on Windows.

### Version stamping

Version, commit, and build date are injected via `-ldflags` at release time:

```sh
go build -ldflags "\
  -X main.version=$(git describe --tags --always) \
  -X main.commit=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \
  -X main.date=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
  -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
```

Check what you have with:

```sh
intropy version
```

## Quickstart

### Scaffold your first integration

```sh
# Inspect a template before you scaffold it
intropy template show hello-world

# Render it into a new directory
intropy int create hello-world -o ./my-integration   # -o is --out-dir here
```

## Command overview

```
intropy
├── int                    Manage integrations
│   ├── create <template>      Scaffold a new integration from a template
│   ├── show [dir]             Show the integration scaffolded at a directory
│   └── list [dir]             List scaffolded integrations under a directory
├── template               Inspect the Intropy template library
│   ├── list                   List the templates in the library
│   └── show <template>        Show a template's manifest and parameter schema
├── sys                    Manage integration systems
│   └── create                 Assemble scaffolded integrations into a system host
├── manifests              Inspect, render, and create Kubernetes manifests
│   ├── inspect                Inspect the deployment model derived from a system topology
│   ├── render                 Render a system's manifests as YAML
│   └── create                 Create missing manifests on a GitOps review branch
├── deploy                 Move components between environments via the GitOps repository
│   ├── pin <component> [ver]  Pin a component's image digest into an environment
│   ├── promote <component>    Copy the digests one environment runs into another
│   ├── diff <component>       Show the rendered change a sync would apply
│   ├── status <component>     Show what every environment runs, side by side
│   └── sync <component>       Apply an environment's pending change through ArgoCD
├── release                Publish and inspect immutable release manifests
│   ├── create <component>     Publish a release manifest and push a git tag
│   ├── list <component>       List the releases published for a component
│   └── view <component> <ver> Read a published release manifest
├── dashboard [dir]        Browse the integrations scaffolded under dir
└── version                Print version information
```

Run any command with `--help` for full flag documentation.

## Templates (`intropy template`)

### List templates

See what the template library publishes:

```sh
intropy template list
intropy template list --template-version v1.2.0
intropy template list -o json
```

Without `--template-version`, the latest GitHub release is listed.

### Show a template

Inspect what parameters a template accepts before scaffolding it:

```sh
intropy template show hello-world
intropy template show hello-world --template-version v1.2.0
intropy template show hello-world -o json   # machine-readable; same schema Backstage renders
```

## Integrations (`intropy int`)

### Create an integration

```sh
intropy int create hello-world --out-dir ./my-integration
```

Name the integration and scaffold it in one step. `-n/--name` sets the template's
`name` parameter (so you're not prompted for it) and, unless `-o/--out-dir` is given,
defaults the output directory to the kebab-cased name — `OrderSync` scaffolds into
`./order-sync`, the same normalization `sys create` applies. With neither flag, the
resolved `name` parameter kebab-cases the same way, so a run that answers the prompts
needs no directory decision at all. `-o/--out-dir` always wins when given — the same
split as `dotnet new`, where `-o` is the literal output location and `-n` only names
the artifacts.

> **Note:** in `int create` and `sys create`, `--output json` selects the result document
> on stdout like everywhere else in the CLI. `-o` always means `--out-dir` here.

```sh
# scaffolds into ./orders and sets name=orders (-n OrderSync would scaffold ./order-sync)
intropy int create hello-world -n orders

# -o/--out-dir overrides the output directory: scaffolds into ./order-extractor with name=OrderExtractor
intropy int create hello-world -n OrderExtractor -o ./order-extractor
```

Provide parameter values inline, from files, or interactively:

```sh
# inline
intropy int create hello-world -o ./out --set name=orders --set owner=team-x

# from a values file (repeatable; use - for stdin)
intropy int create hello-world -o ./out -f values.yaml

# disable interactive prompts (fail fast on missing required values)
intropy int create hello-world -o ./out --no-input -f values.yaml

# print the machine-readable result document to stdout (same as every other command)
intropy int create hello-world -o ./out --output json
```

Use `--force` to render into a non-empty directory.

`int create` also writes a scaffold record to `.intropy/scaffold.json` inside
the new integration — the template name, the exact release version, and the
resolved parameter values. Commit it: later commands read it to reproduce
decisions made at scaffold time.

### Show an integration

Print the scaffold record of the integration at a directory — which template
rendered it, from which release, with which values:

```sh
# current directory (searched upward)
intropy int show

# an explicit project directory
intropy int show ./my-integration

# the record unchanged, for scripts
intropy int show -o json
```

### List scaffolded integrations

Discover every integration under a directory tree — each project is
identified by its committed `.intropy/scaffold.json` record:

```sh
# walk down from the current directory
intropy int list

# or from an explicit root
intropy int list ~/dev/integrations

# machine-readable, including the pinned source and scaffold values
intropy int list -o json
```

The walk skips `.git`, `node_modules`, `bin` and `dist`, and doesn't descend
into a project once matched (projects don't nest). Projects with an unreadable
record are reported as warnings on stderr without hiding the rest.

## Systems (`intropy sys`)

### Assemble a system host

Run from the workspace root that holds your scaffolded integrations:

```sh
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host   # -o is --out-dir here
```

The command reads before it writes: it scans the workspace for the
`.intropy/scaffold.json` records the integration scaffolds left behind,
validates them into a system model, and passes the assembled values to
the `system-host` template (a .NET Aspire AppHost), which renders the
whole declaration — `Topics.cs` defines each topic once as a
`TopicRef<T>`, `Ports.cs` defines each edge block's port to the outside
world (its deployed transport shape — connection values are deployment
configuration), and the `ISystemDefinition` class wires every extractor
and loader to its topic plus its port (`.From(...)` on extractors,
`.To(...)` on loaders) and the platform services (`.Uses(...)`). The workspace's shared contracts project (template role
`shared-library`, typically `Contracts/`) is referenced from the host's
project file, never declared as a component. A contracts project is only
needed when the system has topics: a host of transactional integrations
alone renders with no `Topics.cs` and no contracts reference, and a
topic-bearing system whose workspace lacks one gets it scaffolded by the
host template itself.

The generated development definition (`<Project>Development.cs`) owns the
local-run picture: it mocks the platform services from the skeleton's
OpenAPI documents and resolves each port to a drop folder under the
host's `test/` directory, so the assembled system runs end-to-end with
zero external configuration — drop a file into `test/<name>-source/`,
collect the result from `test/<name>-destination/`.

`-n` accepts PascalCase or kebab-case — `OrderFlow` kebab-cases to
`order-flow`, the system's name. Unlike `int create` there are no `--set`
or values flags: the CLI assembles every value from the scaffold records,
and the template never prompts.

This CLI renders against the current `system-host` release; pin an older
one with `--template-version`.

```sh
# default output directory: the kebab-cased name (./order-flow)
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow

# pin the system-host template release
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host --template-version v1.5.0

# machine-readable result document with the assembled model
intropy sys create -n OrderFlow -o system-host --output json
```

> **Note:** as with `int create`, `--output json` prints the result document to stdout.

Records without a `blockKind` (scaffolded by an older CLI) or with an
unsupported block kind are skipped with a warning listing the supported
kinds. The assembled kinds:

- **extractor / loader** — topic blocks. Their records carry `topic`,
  `contract`, and one optional `port`; a record without a `port` value
  keeps its component but gets no `From`/`To`.
- **transactional-integration** — a port-to-port block with no topic. Its
  record carries `fromPort` and `toPort`; both are required, and a missing
  one fails the assembly. The generated system class wires it as
  `.From(Ports.X).To(Ports.Y)`.

Validate the result from the host directory with `dotnet run -- check`.

## Kubernetes manifests (`intropy manifests`)

Manifest generation is split by intent: inspect the derived model, render a
complete YAML stream for local development, or create missing GitOps source
files for one environment.

### Inspect the deployment model

```sh
intropy manifests inspect
intropy manifests inspect --system order-flow -o json
```

`inspect` reads the system topology, scaffold records, and template release. It
reports components, workloads, ports, and the release's available local
fixtures without rendering or writing anything.

### Render local YAML

```sh
intropy manifests render --env local | kubectl apply -f -
intropy manifests render --env local --binding fno=http
```

Each topology port needs a local fixture. Repeat
`--binding <port>=<fixture>` for reproducible and non-interactive renders.
When a choice is missing in an interactive terminal, a Huh selector asks for it;
the selection applies to that render only and is never persisted.

Only YAML is written to stdout. Progress, prompts, warnings, and errors go to
stderr, and the complete render is buffered and validated before stdout is
written. A failed render therefore cannot apply an incomplete prefix through
the pipe. Use `--namespace` to change the target namespace and repeat `--image`
for local image overrides.

### Create GitOps manifests

```sh
intropy manifests create --env prod --dry-run
intropy manifests create --env prod --diff
intropy manifests create --env prod
```

# Next-feature recommendation for intropy-cli

## Context

Asked: "what should the next feature be?" — assessment only, no code changes.

State of the CLI (2026-08-29, branch `feature/flow-slot-create`):

- Command surface: `int create|show|list`, `template list|show`, `sys create|update`,
  `manifests inspect|render|create`, `deploy pin|promote|diff|status|sync`,
  `release create|list|show`, `dashboard`, `version`. Hidden stubs: `int describe`, `int local`.
- This branch turns the dashboard flow view into a build-and-run surface: create
  components from slots, sync the host (`sys create|update`), **start/stop the host**
  (`internal/dashboard/run.go`), **seed test files** (`internal/dashboard/testdata.go`),
  workspace facts/suggestions shared with `int create`.
- Two designed-but-unbuilt plans exist: `docs/plans/deploy-show-command.md` and
  `docs/plans/2026-01-15-001-feat-config-contexts-plan.md` (untracked, written today).

## Recommendation (ranked)

### 1. `intropy sys run` — headless local run loop (top pick)

Problem: the branch put run supervision and fixture seeding *only* behind the
dashboard's HTTP handlers. The CLI cannot start a host, seed a port, or read the
run log. That inverts the project's own rule (dashboard reuses command entry
points; it never owns behavior a command lacks), and it leaves agents/CI — the
intropy-build skills verify via raw `dotnet run -- check` and hand-copied
fixtures — without a one-command scaffold → assemble → run → seed → observe loop.

Shape:
- Lift `dotnetStart`/`runHandle`/`logPump`/`stopHandle`/process-group code from
  `internal/dashboard/run.go` and `copySeedFile`/`systemHostDir`/`devRootPath`/
  `confineUnder` from `internal/dashboard/testdata.go` into `internal/system`
  (or a new `internal/run`). Dashboard handlers become thin callers.
- `intropy sys run [dir]` — start the host, stream stdout/stderr to stderr, stop
  on Ctrl+C (SIGTERM → 5s → SIGKILL, whole process group). `--seed <port>=<fixture>`
  (repeatable) copies fixtures after the host reports ready; `--output json`
  prints the run record (pid, host dir, seeded files, exit).
- Optionally `sys seed <port> <fixture>` as a standalone verb for a host started
  elsewhere.
- Add `run` (and `seed` if split) to the AGENTS.md verb table with its reason.

Why first: closes the loop the whole skill suite targets; most of the code is
already written and tested on this branch; it should be done before the
dashboard-only version ossifies.

### 2. `intropy deploy show`

Fully designed in `docs/plans/deploy-show-command.md`: read-only, declaration-only
description of the GitOps repo (environments in promotion order, systems/components,
secret-bearing resources) plus a dashboard section consuming the same JSON. No open
design questions; pick-up-and-build.

### 3. Config contexts (`intropy context use|list|show`)

Plan written today; the natural pick if multi-customer switching is the current
pain. Note the deferred item: wiring `organization` into `int create`/`sys create`
defaults is a separate follow-up — the mechanism alone changes nothing visible.

## Hygiene worth folding into whichever ships next

- README command overview drift: lists `release view` (code: `release show`), omits `sys update`.
- `int local` / `int describe` stubs are marked "remove next release".
- `sys update` never deletes; a `sys remove <component>` (or equivalent) is the
  named future command.
- Thinnest test spots by file: `internal/registry` (index/pull/push/resolve),
  `internal/deploy` manifests_*/session/snapshot.

## Verification (for whichever is chosen)

- `make build && go test ./...`
- For #1: `intropy sys run --seed <port>=<fixture>` against a scaffolded workspace
  produces output in `test/<port>-destination/`; dashboard start/stop/seed still
  work through the shared code; Ctrl+C leaves no listening dotnet process.
